children: The artificial intelligence infrastructure boom could require $10.3T of U.S. investment through 2032, with a growing share of the financial risk shifting away from Big Tech balance sheets and into less-transparent financing structures, according to new Brookings Institution research.

Columbia Business School professor Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh estimates spending on datacenters, power systems, networking and specialized computing equipment will average about 3.6% of U.S. GDP annually from 2025 through 2032.
Relative to the economy, that would make the AI buildout larger than historic U.S. investment booms in railroads, highways, electrification and telecom.
The scale is increasingly straining the traditional model in which hyperscalers finance infrastructure largely with their own cash flows and corporate debt.
is projected to exceed $800 billion in 2026, surpassing their combined operating cash flow for the first time, the paper said.

As a result, financing is moving toward leases, joint ventures, project debt, private credit, securitizations and special-purpose vehicles. Those structures broaden the pool of available capital but can also shift leverage and contingent liabilities away from hyperscalers' reported balance sheets, making overall exposure harder to assess.

Meta's Hyperion datacenter provides one example. Brookings said the roughly $30B project was financed with about $27B of external debt after Meta sold an 80% equity stake to Blue Owl. The resulting project-level debt-to-asset ratio was roughly 90%, even though Meta itself maintained far lower corporate leverage.

The risks remain tied to the underlying economics of AI, including demand for compute, rapid hardware obsolescence, power availability, construction delays and the credit quality of a relatively small number of hyperscale tenants.

Van Nieuwerburgh stopped short of describing the buildout as a systemic financial threat comparable with previous credit booms. But he warned that increasingly complex off-balance-sheet structures could make correlated exposures difficult to identify before a downturn, arguing that improved measurement and transparency should be a policy priority while the industry's capital structure is still developing.

title: AI buildout could cost $10.3T as financing risks move off Big Tech balance sheets
